questions.q: Which Hungarian obstetrician championed handwashing in the 1840s and died in an asylum?
questions.e: Proven right after his death. Wash your hands.

questions.q: Which bone is the only one in the body that doesn’t articulate with another bone?
questions.e: Held in place by muscles and ligaments alone.

questions.q: William Withering described which heart drug in 1785, from the foxglove plant?
questions.e: Accept digoxin.

questions.q: ‘Saturday night palsy’ is a compression injury of which nerve?
questions.e: Arm draped over a chair after a big night. Wrist drop follows.

questions.q: Which fungus causes ‘rose gardener’s disease’?
questions.e: Sporotrichosis, from a thorn prick.

questions.q: In the early seasons of ‘Grey’s Anatomy’, what was the hospital called?
questions.e: Later Seattle Grace Mercy West, then Grey Sloan Memorial.

questions.q: The word ‘malaria’ comes from Italian for what?
questions.e: Mala aria. Blame the swamps, not the mosquitoes.

questions.q: How long does a red blood cell live, on average?
questions.e: Red cells live about 120 days, then the spleen and liver recycle them. That’s why HbA1c reflects roughly the last three months of blood glucose.

questions.q: Which US president secretly had Addison’s disease?
questions.e: JFK had Addison’s disease (adrenal failure), kept quiet during his presidency and managed with steroids.

questions.q: What is the photic sneeze reflex better known as, by its acronym?
questions.e: Sneezing on stepping into bright light. Autosomal dominant. Bless you.

questions.q: Who shared the 1923 Nobel Prize for the discovery of insulin?
questions.e: Banting shared his half with Charles Best.

questions.q: What is the most common primary malignant bone tumour in adolescents?
questions.e: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in teenagers, typically around the knee during growth spurts.

questions.q: Roughly how many litres of blood does the heart pump per minute at rest?
questions.e: Cardiac output: heart rate × stroke volume.

questions.q: Which poison is classically said to smell of bitter almonds?
questions.e: Not everyone can smell it. It’s genetic.

questions.q: Which Persian physician wrote ‘The Canon of Medicine’ around 1025?
questions.e: Ibn Sina. A standard textbook for 600 years.

questions.q: What is the longest nerve in the human body?
questions.e: The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back down the back of the leg, and is about as thick as a thumb at its widest.

questions.q: Aspirin’s ancestor came from the bark of which tree?
questions.e: Salicylates, from Salix.

questions.q: Which creator of Sherlock Holmes was also a doctor?
questions.e: Holmes was based on his teacher, Dr Joseph Bell.

questions.q: What are the transverse grooves across the nails after a severe illness called?
questions.e: Beau’s lines are dents across the nails where growth paused during a severe illness. They grow out over months.

questions.q: What is the longest word in major English dictionaries, a lung disease from fine silica dust?
questions.e: Invented in 1935 to be the longest word. It worked.

questions.q: Who gave the first public demonstration of ether anaesthesia, in Boston in 1846?
questions.e: At Massachusetts General. The room is now the Ether Dome.

questions.q: What is the smallest skeletal muscle in the body?
questions.e: It dampens the stapes against loud noise.

questions.q: Drugs ending in ‘-pril’ belong to which class?
questions.e: Ramipril, perindopril and friends. Hello, dry cough.

questions.q: Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs are classic signs of what?
questions.e: Classic, but not very sensitive.

questions.q: Which bacterium causes cat-scratch disease?
questions.e: Bartonella henselae, usually from a kitten scratch or bite, causes swollen lymph nodes near the scratch.

questions.q: Who played paediatrician Doug Ross in ‘ER’?
questions.e: George Clooney played Dr Doug Ross, the paediatrician, in ER from 1994.

questions.q: ‘Influenza’ comes from the Italian for what?
questions.e: Of the stars, supposedly.

questions.q: Which hormone does the pineal gland secrete?
questions.e: The pineal gland releases melatonin as light fades, helping set the sleep-wake cycle.

questions.q: Which physicist lived with motor neurone disease for over 50 years?
questions.e: Diagnosed at 21. Died at 76.

questions.q: What is a borborygmus?
questions.e: Plural: borborygmi.

questions.q: Who shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Watson and Crick for DNA’s structure?
questions.e: Rosalind Franklin had died in 1958.

questions.q: Reed–Sternberg cells are the hallmark of which cancer?
questions.e: The ‘owl’s eye’ cells.

questions.q: How many bones are in one human hand and wrist?
questions.e: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges.

questions.q: Which plant poison was used to execute Socrates?
questions.e: Socrates was sentenced to death in Athens in 399 BC and drank poison hemlock.

questions.q: Who pioneered antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in the 1860s?
questions.e: Yes, Listerine.

questions.q: What are you actually hitting when you bang your ‘funny bone’?
questions.e: Not funny. Not a bone.

questions.q: What is the antidote to paracetamol overdose?
questions.e: Accept NAC or acetylcysteine.

questions.q: In ‘Scrubs’, who is JD’s reluctant mentor?
questions.e: Dr Perry Cox, played by John C. McGinley, mentors JD while insisting he doesn’t.

questions.q: Which spots inside the mouth are an early sign of measles?
questions.e: Grains of salt on a red background.

questions.q: What is the medical term for brain freeze?
questions.e: From eating ice cream too fast.

questions.q: Worimi man Kelvin Kong became Australia’s first Aboriginal surgeon. What is his specialty?
questions.e: Accept ENT or otolaryngology. He champions ear health for Aboriginal children, who have some of the world’s highest rates of chronic middle-ear infection.

questions.q: Which organ contains the islets of Langerhans?
questions.e: The islets of Langerhans are clusters of hormone-making cells in the pancreas. Their beta cells make insulin.

questions.q: Sildenafil (Viagra) was first trialled for which condition?
questions.e: The side effect stole the show.

questions.q: Erb’s palsy is an injury to which nerve network?
questions.e: Upper roots, C5–C6. ‘Waiter’s tip’ posture.

questions.q: Which virus causes both chickenpox and shingles?
questions.e: It never really leaves.

questions.q: Which city is the emergency department in ‘The Pitt’ set in?
questions.e: The Pitt is set in the emergency department of a Pittsburgh trauma hospital, with each episode covering one hour of a shift.

questions.q: ‘Quarantine’ comes from the Italian for what?
questions.e: Quaranta giorni. Venice made plague ships wait.

questions.q: What is the normal pH range of arterial blood?
questions.e: Normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45. Below that is acidaemia, above is alkalaemia. Also accept 7.4.

questions.q: Which US president was paralysed by an illness diagnosed as polio in 1921?
questions.e: Some now suspect Guillain–Barré syndrome.

questions.q: What is the medical term for hiccups?
questions.e: Singultus is the medical term for hiccups, from the Latin for a sob.

questions.q: Which chemist, who never finished a PhD, shared the 1988 Nobel Prize for developing drugs including azathioprine and aciclovir?
questions.e: Accept Trudy Elion. Early on she was turned away from lab jobs for being a woman.

questions.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes beriberi?
questions.e: Beriberi is thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, historically from diets of polished white rice. Also accept B1.

questions.q: Roughly how many protein-coding genes are in the human genome?
questions.e: Fewer than a grape has.

questions.q: Which metal caused the ‘mad hatter’ symptoms in hat makers?
questions.e: Used to treat felt.

questions.q: Who was known as ‘the Lady with the Lamp’?
questions.e: Also a pioneering statistician.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart has the thickest wall?
questions.e: The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body, so its wall is about three times thicker than the right’s.

questions.q: Which chemotherapy drug was first isolated from the Pacific yew tree?
questions.e: Accept Taxol.

questions.q: Which 1966 film shrinks a medical team to travel through a man’s bloodstream?
questions.e: In Fantastic Voyage (1966), a shrunken submarine crew travels through a scientist’s bloodstream to remove a brain clot.

questions.q: Virchow’s triad describes the causes of what?
questions.e: Stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability.

questions.q: Which parts of the body have the highest density of sweat glands?
questions.e: Hence sweaty palms in exams.

questions.q: In 1886, which woman graduated from the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania, becoming one of India’s first women doctors of Western medicine?
questions.e: Accept Anandi Gopal Joshi. She died of tuberculosis at 21, months after returning home.

questions.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.e: In the middle ear. About 3 mm.

questions.q: Semaglutide (Ozempic) mimics which gut hormone?
questions.e: Glucagon-like peptide-1.

questions.q: Whose sign is calf pain on dorsiflexion of the foot, once taught for DVT?
questions.e: Now considered unreliable.

questions.q: ‘Typhoid Mary’ was a carrier of which bacterium?
questions.e: A cook. Never ill herself.

questions.q: What was Derek Shepherd’s nickname in ‘Grey’s Anatomy’?
questions.e: Dr Derek Shepherd, played by Patrick Dempsey, was nicknamed McDreamy.

questions.q: ‘Vaccine’ comes from the Latin for which animal?
questions.e: Vacca. Jenner used cowpox.

questions.q: Which ion mainly sets the resting membrane potential of cells?
questions.e: Potassium leaking out of cells through potassium channels mainly sets the resting membrane potential, around −70 mV.

questions.q: Patient H.M. lost the ability to form new memories after surgery removed which structures?
questions.e: Both medial temporal lobes, in 1953.

questions.q: What is the medical term for goosebumps?
questions.e: Accept cutis anserina.

questions.q: Which two scientists won the 2005 Nobel Prize for showing H. pylori causes ulcers?
questions.e: Marshall drank a culture to prove it.

questions.q: The Philadelphia chromosome is a swap between which two chromosomes?
questions.e: The BCR-ABL fusion gene.

questions.q: Roughly what is an average adult’s total lung capacity?
questions.e: Total lung capacity in an average adult is about 6 litres, a little less in women and smaller adults. Accept 5 to 6 litres.

questions.q: Which toxin, one of the most lethal known, is injected to smooth wrinkles?
questions.e: Botulinum toxin is among the most lethal substances known, yet tiny doses relax muscles to smooth wrinkles and treat spasticity.

questions.q: In 1854, John Snow removed the handle of a cholera-spreading pump on which London street?
questions.e: The birth of epidemiology.

questions.q: What is the largest internal organ?
questions.e: The liver is the largest internal organ at about 1.5 kg. The skin is the largest organ overall.

questions.q: Morphine is named after which Greek god?
questions.e: God of dreams.

questions.q: What is the hospital called in ‘Scrubs’?
questions.e: Scrubs is set at Sacred Heart Hospital, a fictional teaching hospital.

questions.q: Cushing’s, Addison’s and Conn’s syndromes all involve which gland?
questions.e: All three are adrenal conditions: Cushing’s (too much cortisol), Addison’s (too little) and Conn’s (too much aldosterone).

questions.q: Which hormone was the first medicine made using recombinant DNA?
questions.e: Human insulin, approved in 1982.

questions.q: Which Paris obstetrician introduced incubators for premature babies in 1880, inspired by chicken incubators at the zoo?
questions.e: The poultry incubators were at the Jardin d’Acclimatation.

questions.q: Which fetal vessel joins the pulmonary artery to the aorta, and often stays open in premature babies?
questions.e: Its remnant is the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.q: Which steroid did Liggins and Howie give mothers in their 1972 Auckland trial to mature preterm babies’ lungs?
questions.e: One of the great trials in obstetrics.

questions.q: The Ballard score estimates what in a newborn?
questions.e: From physical and neuromuscular signs.

questions.q: Which bacterium, carried harmlessly by many pregnant women, is a leading cause of early newborn sepsis?
questions.e: Streptococcus agalactiae. Accept GBS.

questions.q: Which BBC drama follows midwives and nuns in Poplar, in London’s East End, from the late 1950s?
questions.e: Based on Jennifer Worth’s memoirs.

questions.q: ‘Neonate’ comes from Greek and Latin roots meaning what?
questions.e: Neos, new; natus, born.

questions.q: Fetal haemoglobin has two alpha chains and two of which other chain?
questions.e: It grabs oxygen more tightly than adult haemoglobin.

questions.q: Which scientist, born prematurely on Christmas Day 1642, was said to be small enough to fit in a quart pot?
questions.e: His mother’s description. He lived to 84.

questions.q: What is the medical term for a baby’s first stool?
questions.e: From the Greek for poppy juice, after its dark colour.

questions.q: Who won the 2010 Nobel Prize for developing IVF?
questions.e: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby, was born in 1978.

questions.q: ‘Hyaline membrane disease’ is an old name for which condition of premature babies?
questions.e: Caused by a lack of surfactant. Accept RDS.

questions.q: Below what birth weight is a baby classed as low birth weight?
questions.e: Accept 2.5 kg. Under 1,500 g is very low birth weight.

questions.q: Which antibiotic caused ‘grey baby syndrome’ in newborns?
questions.e: Newborn livers can’t clear it fast enough.

questions.q: In 1959, which paediatrician showed that premature babies with breathing distress lack lung surfactant?
questions.e: With Jere Mead. Her finding led to surfactant treatment, which has saved huge numbers of premature babies.

questions.q: Which opening between the atria normally closes soon after birth?
questions.e: It stays open in about 1 in 4 adults.

questions.q: Which drug, also found in coffee, is used for apnoea of prematurity?
questions.e: As caffeine citrate. Some of the world’s smallest caffeine users.

questions.q: In ‘Friends’, who gives birth in ‘The One with the Birth’?
questions.e: Ross’s ex-wife, to baby Ben.

questions.q: Which newborn reflex makes a baby fling out its arms when startled?
questions.e: Named after Austrian paediatrician Ernst Moro.

questions.q: Which Bogotá paediatrician introduced kangaroo mother care in 1978, when incubators were scarce?
questions.e: Parents became the incubator. Happy World Prematurity Day.

questions.q: Which Welsh GP coined the ‘inverse care law’ in The Lancet in 1971?
questions.e: Good care varies inversely with need. Accept Tudor Hart or Tudor-Hart. Fifty-odd years on, the law remains annoyingly unrepealed.

questions.q: The 4S trial (Lancet, 1994) cut all-cause mortality by about 30% using which statin?
questions.e: The Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study, 4,444 patients. If you said atorvastatin, you’re a few years early.

questions.q: Which pressure-injury risk scale scores sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction and shear?
questions.e: Bergstrom and Braden, 1987. Lower score, higher risk. Norton and Waterlow are lovely, but wrong.

questions.q: Which child psychiatrist, a Palyku woman, is recognised as the first Indigenous Australian to become a doctor?
questions.e: UWA, 1983. Later a professor and the AFL’s first Indigenous commissioner. Accept Milroy.

questions.q: ISIS-2 (1988) showed a mortality benefit in suspected MI from aspirin and which other drug?
questions.e: Together they cut vascular deaths by about 40%. Accept SK. Alteplase wasn’t invited.

questions.q: Levetiracetam works by binding which synaptic vesicle protein?
questions.e: Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A. Accept SV2A or synaptic vesicle protein 2A. ‘Sodium channels’ is the answer to a different drug.

questions.q: Which roll manoeuvre, nicknamed the ‘barbecue roll’, treats horizontal-canal BPPV?
questions.e: The patient turns in 90° steps, like a sausage. Accept Lempert or roll manoeuvre. Epley is for the posterior canal, sorry.

questions.q: Which sign says abdominal tenderness that persists or worsens when the patient tenses the abdominal wall points to a wall source?
questions.e: Tensed muscles shield the viscera, so pain that persists comes from the wall itself, e.g. nerve entrapment. Accept Carnett. The surgeon can put the knife down.

questions.q: In Light’s criteria, pleural fluid LDH above what fraction of the upper limit of normal serum LDH suggests an exudate?
questions.e: The other two: protein ratio over 0.5 and LDH ratio over 0.6. Accept 2/3 or 0.67. A half is the protein one.

questions.q: Which syndrome is congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina with normal ovaries and karyotype 46,XX?
questions.e: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser. Accept MRKH or Müllerian agenesis. Presents as primary amenorrhoea with normal breasts and hair.

questions.q: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia by blocking which receptor?
questions.e: It stops calcium leaking from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Accept RyR1 or ryanodine. Not the nicotinic receptor, that’s the suxamethonium talking.

questions.q: Which retrovirus has the world’s highest recorded prevalence among Aboriginal adults in central Australia?
questions.e: Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1, a strain called subtype C. Linked to bronchiectasis and adult T-cell leukaemia. Accept HTLV-1 or human T-cell lymphotropic virus.

questions.q: Upsloping ST depression with tall, symmetrical precordial T waves suggests proximal LAD occlusion. Whose T waves?
questions.e: De Winter T waves, described in 2008. A STEMI equivalent. Wellens’ is the other LAD eponym, but its T waves go the wrong way.

questions.q: Konzo, a sudden permanent spastic paraparesis in sub-Saharan Africa, is linked to eating poorly processed what?
questions.e: Cyanogens, mainly linamarin. Worst in the DRC during drought, war and famine. Accept cassava or manioc.

questions.q: Which autosomal recessive syndrome pairs profound congenital deafness with a long QT interval?
questions.e: Usually KCNQ1 or KCNE1. Accept JLN. Romano-Ward is the autosomal dominant one with normal hearing.

questions.q: Which syndrome is painful ophthalmoplegia from granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus, melting with steroids?
questions.e: A diagnosis of exclusion. Accept Tolosa-Hunt. If you said Gradenigo, wrong bit of the skull.

questions.q: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, which turns muscle to bone, is caused by mutations in which gene?
questions.e: Usually R206H, in the BMP type I receptor also called ALK2. Accept ACVR1 or ALK2. Never biopsy the lumps: injury triggers new bone.

questions.q: Which muscle is the only abductor of the vocal folds?
questions.e: ‘Posterior cricoarytenoid pulls them apart.’ Lose both and the airway shuts. Accept PCA. Lateral cricoarytenoid does the exact opposite.

questions.q: Which French paediatric cardiologist spotted the extra chromosome in Down syndrome, though a colleague got the credit?
questions.e: Her cultures, 1958. Jérôme Lejeune was first author in 1959, and Gautier’s name was misspelt. Accept Gautier.

questions.q: Which eponymous nerve, a branch of the vagus, makes some patients cough when you clean their ear canal?
questions.e: The auricular branch of the vagus, hence Arnold’s ear-cough reflex. Accept Arnold or auricular branch of the vagus. The ear syringe is innocent.

questions.q: Conjoined twins arise when one embryo divides late. After about which day post-fertilisation does division come too late for twins to separate fully?
questions.e: Split by day 3: two placentas. Days 4 to 8: shared placenta. Days 8 to 12: shared amnion. After about day 13: joined. Accept 13 to 15.

questions.q: The ending ‘-pagus’, as in thoracopagus and craniopagus, comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.e: From pagos, something fixed. Accept fixed or joined. Thoracopagus: joined at the chest.

questions.q: Which five-stage system is used to grade twin-twin transfusion syndrome?
questions.e: Stage I to V, from Rubén Quintero’s 1999 paper. It’s a problem of shared placentas, so monochorionic twins only.

questions.q: A ‘lambda’ or ‘twin peak’ sign on first-trimester ultrasound means the twins have what chorionicity?
questions.e: Placental tissue wedges between the membranes. The flat ‘T sign’ means monochorionic. Spot it early, it gets harder later.

questions.q: Chang and Eng Bunker, conjoined brothers who became American farmers, were born in 1811 in which present-day country?
questions.e: Then called Siam, which gave us an old term now retired. ‘Conjoined’ is the word to use.

questions.q: A patient known as L.M. saw poured tea as frozen in mid-air and traffic as jumping from place to place. Name the condition.
questions.e: Motion blindness, after damage around area V5/MT. Josef Zihl’s team described her in 1983. Accept cerebral akinetopsia.

questions.q: Which Maine midwife’s diary (1785 to 1812) recorded more than 800 births and inspired a Pulitzer-winning history?
questions.e: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich’s A Midwife’s Tale, 1990. Accept Ballard.

questions.q: At which military hospital, in present-day Istanbul, did Florence Nightingale’s nurses work during the Crimean War?
questions.e: The Selimiye Barracks in Üsküdar. Accept Selimiye or Üsküdar. Yes, the lamp was real.

questions.q: Which Edinburgh obstetrician tested vapours on himself and his dinner guests, then introduced chloroform anaesthesia in 1847?
questions.e: They all ended up under the table. Accept Simpson. House rules for dinner parties have improved.

questions.q: Loss-of-function variants in which skin barrier protein are a major risk factor for atopic eczema and ichthyosis vulgaris?
questions.e: The FLG gene. ‘Filament-aggregating protein’, if you’re asked at a party. You won’t be.

questions.q: Who received the first multichannel cochlear implant, from Graeme Clark’s team in Melbourne in 1978?
questions.e: He’d lost his hearing in a car accident. Accept Saunders. Clark gets the credit, Saunders did the bravest bit.

questions.q: Which French surgeon, author of Le Chirurgien Dentiste (1728), is called the father of modern dentistry?
questions.e: Accept Fauchard. He pushed sugar’s role in decay, long before anyone wanted to hear it.

questions.q: What is the chart called that plots daily quality-control results against mean and standard deviation lines?
questions.e: Levey and Jennings, 1950, borrowing from Shewhart’s factory charts. Accept Levey-Jennings or Shewhart.

questions.q: What term describes genuine expert uncertainty about which treatment is better, the ethical basis for randomising patients?
questions.e: Benjamin Freedman, NEJM, 1987. Accept equipoise. ‘We have no idea’ is not accepted, though it’s close.

questions.q: Which doctrine allows a treatment given to relieve suffering even if it may foreseeably shorten life, provided relief is the intention?
questions.e: Usually traced to Thomas Aquinas. Accept double effect.

questions.q: Which Māori health model, described by Sir Mason Durie, likens wellbeing to a meeting house with four walls?
questions.e: Physical, spiritual, family and mental health. Take away one wall and the house leans.

questions.q: What is the eponymous name for a relative afferent pupillary defect found on the swinging torch test?
questions.e: Robert Marcus Gunn, Scottish ophthalmologist. Accept RAPD with the name. The torch swings, the pupil seems to dilate.

questions.q: In 1937, more than 100 Americans died after taking an antibiotic syrup made with which solvent?
questions.e: The Elixir Sulfanilamide disaster, which led to the 1938 US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act. Accept DEG. Sweet, soluble and a kidney poison, so no wonder nobody tasted the problem.

questions.q: Which 2010 trial, in men who have sex with men and trans women across six countries, first showed daily oral tablets could prevent HIV?
questions.e: Tenofovir and emtricitabine cut HIV infection by 44%, more with good adherence. Published in NEJM. Accept PrEP only if you can name the trial. You can’t. It’s iPrEx.

questions.q: NASA’s Twins Study sent Scott Kelly to space for nearly a year while Mark stayed home. Scott’s telomeres did what surprising thing up there?
questions.e: Everyone expected shortening. They lengthened in flight, then shortened quickly back on Earth. Science, 2019. Space remains weird.

questions.q: In which Finnish region did a 1972 community project, begun after locals petitioned for help with heart disease, become a model for world prevention?
questions.e: Led by Pekka Puska. Less salt, less butter, less smoking, and people took it up. Accept Pohjois-Karjala.

questions.q: Which sugar alcohol, mass-produced from birch in Finland, was tested for caries prevention in the 1970s Turku sugar studies?
questions.e: Scheinin and Mäkinen swapped people’s sugar for it. Hence the chewing gum on every chemist’s counter.

questions.q: Erik von Willebrand, a Helsinki physician, described his bleeding disorder in 1926 in a family from which Finnish islands?
questions.e: Accept Åland. Pseudohaemophilia, he called it, affecting women as well as men.

questions.q: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type is caused by variants in the gene for which slit-diaphragm protein?
questions.e: The NPHS1 gene. One of the Finnish disease heritage, about 36 rare conditions more common there. Accept NPHS1.

questions.q: Sugammadex reverses which neuromuscular blocker by encapsulating it?
questions.e: It’s a modified cyclodextrin, a molecular doughnut. Accept vecuronium too. Not suxamethonium, nice try.

questions.q: Which Colombian neurosurgeon described normal pressure hydrocephalus in 1965?
questions.e: Accept Hakim. With Raymond Adams. Gait, continence, cognition: the classic triad.

questions.q: Four British nurses and midwives founded which society in 1894, the forerunner of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy?
questions.e: Founded to protect the profession’s good name. Accept the gist.

questions.q: Morton’s neuroma is most often found between which two metatarsal heads?
questions.e: Accept the third web space. It feels like standing on a pebble in your sock.

questions.q: Which researcher ran the 1940s Minnesota Starvation Experiment and later championed the Mediterranean diet?
questions.e: Accept Keys. He also developed the K-ration, and the K may or may not be for Keys.

questions.q: What does IDDSI stand for?
questions.e: Eight levels, 0 to 7, from thin drinks to regular food. Accept any version that gets dysphagia in.

questions.q: In 1984 Barry Marshall tested Koch’s postulates the hard way. What did he do?
questions.a: Drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori
questions.e: He got gastritis and a Nobel, eventually. Accept any version of drinking it. His wife had views.

questions.q: What are the ropey eosinophilic inclusions seen in hepatocytes in alcohol-related hepatitis?
questions.e: Tangled keratin filaments. Accept Mallory bodies or Mallory hyaline. Hepatologists would like you to know they’re not specific.

questions.q: In 1954, what ‘oxygenator’ did C. Walton Lillehei use for open-heart surgery on children?
questions.e: Cross-circulation. A parent’s heart and lungs supported the child. The only operation with a potential 200% mortality, its critics said.

questions.q: What paradox describes a trend that appears in several groups but reverses when the groups are combined?
questions.e: Edward Simpson, 1951. Accept Yule-Simpson. Not Homer.

questions.q: Which cardiologist, the first woman to lead the US NIH, coined ‘Yentl syndrome’ in a 1991 NEJM editorial?
questions.e: Women had to look like men to get the same heart care. Accept Healy.

questions.q: Which roundworm can persist for decades through autoinfection, so migrants from endemic areas are screened before steroids?
questions.e: Steroids can trigger fatal hyperinfection. Accept Strongyloides. A worm with very long-term plans.

questions.q: Which UK organisation’s 1976 ‘Fundamental Principles of Disability’ laid the groundwork for the social model?
questions.e: The Union of the Physically Impaired Against Segregation. Accept the full name.

questions.q: Which syndrome, first described in prisoners in 1898, features approximate answers such as 2 + 2 = 5?
questions.e: Sigbert Ganser. The answer is just wrong enough to show you knew it. Vorbeireden, if you’re showing off.

questions.q: Which brain pathway, running from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, is central to reward in addiction?
questions.e: Accept mesolimbic. Not the nigrostriatal one, that’s movement. Mesocortical is its neighbour.

questions.q: Finnish medicine loves a long word. ‘Virtsa’ means urine. What does virtsanpidätyskyvyttömyys mean?
questions.e: Literally ‘urine-holding-ability-lessness’. Accept incontinence. Happy Independence Day, Finland.

questions.q: Which Cleveland surgeon performed the first successful defibrillation of a human heart, on a 14-year-old boy in 1947?
questions.e: Open chest, paddles on the heart, and the boy survived. Beck’s triad is his too. Accept Beck.

questions.q: Which American cardiologist first shocked a human heart back through a closed chest, publishing in 1956?
questions.e: Accept Zoll. The same man took the pacemaker to the skin in 1952. Busy decade.

questions.q: What did Frank Pantridge pioneer in Belfast in the 1960s?
questions.e: With mobile coronary care, taking the shock to the patient. Accept either. The first model ran on car batteries.

questions.q: Which 1960 JAMA paper by Kouwenhoven, Jude and Knickerbocker introduced what now-standard technique?
questions.e: Chest compressions. They spotted it while testing defibrillators on dogs. Accept compressions or CPR.

questions.q: The face of the Resusci Anne training manikin was modelled on a death mask known by which name?
questions.e: An unknown young woman from 1880s Paris. Asmund Laerdal, a Norwegian toymaker, chose it in 1960. Often called the most-kissed face in the world.

questions.q: Commotio cordis, VF from a blow to the chest, needs the hit to land during which part of the ECG?
questions.a: The upslope of the T wave
questions.e: A window of about 10 to 30 ms before the peak. Accept T wave. Terrible luck, in other words.

questions.q: Which Polish-born physician, after his mentor died of VT, invented the implantable defibrillator, first used in a patient in 1980?
questions.e: At Johns Hopkins, with Morton Mower. Accept Mirowski. Colleagues told him it wouldn’t work.

questions.q: Which ‘mother of occupational therapy’ developed habit training?
questions.e: Accept Slagle. A founder of the US professional society, in 1917.

questions.q: The prescription symbol ‘Rx’ is usually said to come from which Latin word?
questions.e: Meaning ‘take’. Accept recipere too. ‘Rex’ is not accepted, even if your GP thinks otherwise.

questions.q: A ‘Jones fracture’ involves which bone?
questions.e: Proximal shaft. Sir Robert Jones described it in 1902, partly from his own, reportedly while dancing.

questions.q: What is the Hall technique for decayed baby molars?
questions.a: Sealing them under preformed metal crowns
questions.e: No drilling, no anaesthetic. Named after Scottish dentist Norna Hall. Children everywhere approve.

questions.q: Which manoeuvre, flexing the mother’s hips sharply onto her abdomen, is a first step for shoulder dystocia?
questions.e: It flattens the lumbosacral angle. Accept McRoberts. Not to be confused with Woods’ screw.

questions.q: Which Australian bush nurse developed hot packs and passive movement for polio paralysis in the 1930s and 40s, against medical opposition?
questions.e: Accept Kenny. Her methods helped shape modern physiotherapy, and Hollywood made a film of her.

questions.q: What are Austin Bradford Hill’s 1965 criteria used for?
questions.a: Judging whether an association is causal
questions.e: Nine viewpoints, from strength to analogy. He never called them criteria. Accept causation.

questions.q: Which acid-fast stain is used to spot Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum?
questions.e: Red rods on a blue background. Accept ZN or auramine. Gram’s stain sends its apologies.

questions.q: Cortical blindness with denial of it, where the person confabulates what they ‘see’, is named after whom?
questions.e: Anton syndrome, 1899. Accept Anton. Sometimes Anton-Babinski.

questions.q: Which Canadian child-first principle, passed by the House of Commons in 2007, honours a boy from Norway House Cree Nation?
questions.e: Jordan River Anderson spent his short life in hospital while governments argued over who should pay for his home care. Care first, argue later.

questions.q: Which partial mu-opioid agonist has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, making it a mainstay for opioid dependence?
questions.e: High affinity, low intrinsic activity. Accept Subutex or Suboxone. Depot versions now run weekly and monthly.

questions.q: Name the three ‘dys-’ symptoms classically associated with endometriosis.
questions.e: Need all three. Period pain, painful sex and painful bowel motions. Diagnosis still takes years on average.

questions.q: Which two physiologists in Geneva showed in 1899 that a strong shock could stop ventricular fibrillation in dogs, 48 years before Beck?
questions.e: Jean-Louis Prévost and Frédéric Batelli. Need both. Accept Battelli. Then everyone forgot for decades.

questions.q: Which 1978 declaration, signed in what is now Kazakhstan, called for ‘health for all by the year 2000’?
questions.e: Primary health care as a human right. Now spelt Almaty. Deadline missed, goal unchanged.

questions.q: Which British epidemiologist chaired the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health, whose 2008 report was ‘Closing the Gap in a Generation’?
questions.e: Also the Whitehall studies. Accept Marmot.

questions.q: In which year did WHO publish its first Model List of Essential Medicines?
questions.e: With 208 medicines. Now updated every two years. No half marks for 1980.

questions.q: Which organisation did Paul Farmer, Ophelia Dahl and Jim Yong Kim co-found to bring care to rural Haiti in 1987?
questions.e: Accept PIH. Farmer’s phrase: ‘the idea that some lives matter less is the root of all that is wrong with the world’.

questions.q: Which Indian doctor used oral rehydration in a 1971 refugee camp during the Bangladesh war, cutting cholera deaths from about 30% to under 4%?
questions.e: Salt, glucose and baking soda from the market, given by families with cups and spoons. Accept Mahalanabis.

questions.q: Who worked with John Flynn in the 1920s to develop the pedal-powered radio that let remote stations call the Flying Doctor?
questions.e: Accept Traeger. Australia’s most useful bicycle-adjacent invention.

questions.q: Which New Zealand-born eye surgeon led trachoma work in Aboriginal communities and set up lens factories in Eritrea and Nepal?
questions.e: Accept Hollows. Cheap lenses, plenty of sight restored, no patience for excuses.

questions.q: In diabetic retinopathy, what are ‘cotton wool spots’?
questions.a: Small infarcts of the nerve fibre layer
questions.e: Backed-up axoplasm from local ischaemia. Accept infarcts or ischaemic patches. Not exudates, that’s the mistake.

questions.q: Which academic coined the phrase ‘social model of disability’ in 1983?
questions.e: The problem is the stairs, not the wheelchair. Accept Oliver, himself a wheelchair user.

questions.q: Which US Public Health Service study, exposed in 1972, left Black men with syphilis untreated for 40 years?
questions.e: Penicillin was withheld for decades. It shaped modern research ethics and left lasting mistrust. Accept Tuskegee.

questions.q: Whose 1972 book Effectiveness and Efficiency inspired a worldwide collaboration of systematic reviews?
questions.e: Accept Cochrane. Scottish doctor and prisoner-of-war camp medic. Very tired of opinions.

questions.q: In a meta-analysis, what does an asymmetric funnel plot suggest?
questions.a: Small-study effects such as publication bias
questions.e: Accept publication bias. Missing small negative studies leave a hole. Journals like good news.

questions.q: Which man received the world’s first human-to-human heart transplant, in Cape Town in 1967?
questions.e: Christiaan Barnard’s patient, a Lithuanian-born grocer. He lived 18 days and died of pneumonia. Accept Washkansky.

questions.q: Which inherited condition gives teeth an opalescent blue-brown look?
questions.e: Enamel’s fine, the dentine isn’t. Can travel with osteogenesis imperfecta, but is often its own gene: DSPP.

questions.q: What is the ‘speech banana’ on an audiogram?
questions.a: The zone where everyday speech sounds fall
questions.e: A banana-shaped region across pitch and loudness. Accept the gist. Sadly no fruit involved.

questions.q: In Westgard quality control rules, what does the 1-3s rule tell you to do?
questions.e: When one control is more than 3 SD from the mean. Accept reject. ‘Rerun it and hope’ is the unofficial rule.

questions.q: Which syndrome, described by Jules Cotard in 1880, involves believing you are dead or missing organs?
questions.e: Accept Cotard. A delusion of negation, rare and often linked to severe depression. It can respond to treatment.

questions.q: Which German pathologist popularised ‘omnis cellula e cellula’, every cell from a cell?
questions.e: Also a politician who said medicine is a social science. Hence his place here. Accept Virchow.

questions.q: Which Berlin physician founded the Institute for Sexual Science in 1919, later destroyed by the Nazis?
questions.e: A pioneering advocate for gay and trans people. Its library was burnt in 1933. Accept Hirschfeld.

questions.q: Which Somali hospital cook, the last person with naturally occurring smallpox in 1977, spent his later years volunteering to end polio?
questions.e: Merca, Somalia. He’d never been vaccinated, and later told families his story. He died in 2013 of malaria, working on polio. Accept Maalin.

questions.q: Which US cohort study, begun in 1948 and still running, gave medicine the phrase ‘risk factor’?
questions.e: Massachusetts. Now on its third generation. Accept Framingham.

questions.q: If R0 is 5, what share of a population must be immune for herd immunity, assuming a perfect vaccine?
questions.e: 1 minus 1/R0. Measles is more like 12 to 18, which is why 95% coverage comes up.

questions.q: Which rector persuaded the village of Eyam in Derbyshire to quarantine itself during the 1665 to 1666 plague?
questions.e: Around a third or more of the village died, and neighbouring towns were spared. His wife Catherine died too. Accept Mompesson.

questions.q: Which sanitary engineer tracked Mary Mallon to the kitchen of a New York family in 1907?
questions.e: Accept Soper. He asked for stool and urine samples. By his account, she chased him off with a carving fork.

questions.q: Louis Pasteur was born on 27 December 1822. Which nine-year-old boy got his rabies vaccine in 1885?
questions.e: From Alsace, bitten by a rabid dog. He survived and later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute.

questions.q: The mumps vaccine strain used since the 1960s is named after who?
questions.e: Maurice Hilleman’s daughter. He swabbed her throat when she got mumps in 1963. Best possible use of a sick day.

questions.q: Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering developed the first effective vaccine for which disease in Michigan in the 1930s?
questions.e: Pertussis. They worked after hours in Grand Rapids. Loney Gordon, a Black chemist, later found a better strain.

questions.q: Ebola was first identified in 1976 in an outbreak centred on a mission hospital in which Zairean village?
questions.e: Now in DR Congo. Reused needles spread it. Sudan had an outbreak the same year. Accept Yambuku only.

questions.q: What does the epidemic preparedness vaccine group CEPI, launched in 2017, stand for?
questions.e: Launched at Davos after Ebola in West Africa. Accept any close version.

questions.q: Which Swedish-born pathologist dug up flu victims at Brevig Mission, Alaska, in 1951 and again in 1997, helping reconstruct the 1918 virus?
questions.e: Accept Hultin. The village council agreed. In 1997 he was 72, using his wife’s garden shears.

questions.q: Which Vienna neurologist described encephalitis lethargica, the 1917 to 1928 epidemic of ‘sleeping sickness’?
questions.e: Accept von Economo. Survivors later inspired Oliver Sacks’s Awakenings. Cause still debated.

questions.q: What does FODMAP stand for?
questions.a: Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides And Polyols
questions.e: Accept the gist. A Monash University idea from Melbourne. Your onion knows what it did.

questions.q: In the ‘PEACE & LOVE’ injury advice, what does LOVE stand for?
questions.e: Dubois and Esculier, BJSM, 2020. Need all four. Goodbye, RICE.

questions.q: During cardiac bypass, what does the ACT test measure?
questions.e: It checks the heparin is working. Accept ACT in full. Nothing to do with theatre.

questions.q: Which naval surgeon ran what is often called the first controlled clinical trial, comparing six scurvy treatments aboard HMS Salisbury in 1747?
questions.e: Citrus won. The navy took over 40 more years to adopt it. Accept Lind.

questions.q: What is the 4AT used for?
questions.e: Four items, under two minutes. Alertness, AMT4, attention, acute change. Accept delirium.

questions.q: Which anaesthetic did dentist Horace Wells try on himself to have a tooth pulled in 1844?
questions.e: Laughing gas. His public demonstration in Boston went badly, so William Morton’s ether took the headlines.

questions.q: Darier’s sign, where rubbing a brown lesion makes it swell and redden, is characteristic of which condition?
questions.e: Urticaria pigmentosa. Accept either. Rub gently, mast cells hold grudges.

questions.q: What was the real name of Broca’s 1861 patient, nicknamed ‘Tan’ for the only word he could say?
questions.e: Accept Leborgne. His full identity was only worked out this century. His brain is still in Paris.

questions.q: Quarantine’s word comes from forty days, but the first known law, a 30-day ‘trentino’ in 1377, was passed in which Adriatic city-state?
questions.e: Now Dubrovnik. Accept either. Travellers from plague areas waited on an islet or at Cavtat. Forty came later.
